title: AC power plugs and sockets
description: Connector used to connect to mains power
wiki_lead:
AC power plugs and sockets connect devices to mains electricity to supply them with electrical power. A plug is the connector attached to an electrically operated device, often via a cable. A socket (also known as a receptacle or outlet) is fixed in place, often on the internal walls of buildings, and is connected to an AC electrical circuit. Inserting ("plugging in") the plug into the socket allows the device to draw power from this circuit.
Plugs and wall-mounted sockets for portable appliances became available in the 1880s, to replace connections to light sockets. A proliferation of types were subsequently developed for both convenience and protection from electrical injury. Electrical plugs and sockets differ from one another in voltage and current rating, shape, size, and connector type. Different standard systems of plugs and sockets are used around the world, and many obsolete socket types are still found in older buildings.
Coordination of technical standards has allowed some types of plug to be used across large regions to facilitate the production and import of electrical appliances and for the convenience of travellers. Some multi-standard sockets allow use of several types of plug. Incompatible sockets and plugs may be used with the help of adaptors, though these may not always provide full safety and performance.

Overview of connections
Single-phase sockets have receptacles for two power pins, one to carry the electrical current from the power source to the connected device (called live, line, or phase pin) and another one to carry it back to the power source (called neutral pin). Many sockets have a third receptacle or pin for a safety connection to earth ground. The plug is a male connector, usually with protruding pins that match the receptacles (female contacts) in a socket. Some plugs also have a female contact, used only for the earth ground connection. Typically no energy is supplied to any exposed pins or terminals on the socket, hence the power pins are always part of the plug rather than the socket. In addition to the recessed contacts of the energised socket, plug and socket systems often have other safety features to reduce the risk of electric shock or damage to appliances.


History

When commercial electric power was first introduced in the 1880s, it was used primarily for lighting. Other portable appliances (such as vacuum cleaners, electric fans, smoothing irons, and curling-tong heaters) were connected to light-bulb sockets. As early as 1885 a two-pin plug and wall socket format was available on the British market. By about 1910 the first three-pin earthed (grounded) plugs appeared. Over time other safety improvements were gradually introduced to the market. One of the first national standards for plugs and wall sockets was enacted in 1915 in the UK.

grok_lead: AC power plugs and sockets are electrical connectors that link appliances and devices to the alternating current (AC) mains supply in buildings, facilitating the safe delivery of electrical power through a male plug inserted into a female receptacle. These devices vary widely in design, with the plug typically featuring pins, blades, or prongs that mate with corresponding slots in the socket to ensure secure, low-resistance contact. The development of AC power plugs and sockets traces back to the late 19th century, amid the electrification of homes and the shift from direct current (DC) to AC systems. Thomas Edison's DC distribution began powering urban areas in the 1880s at around 110 volts, but Nikola Tesla's AC system, patented in 1887, prevailed for its ability to transmit power over long distances with less loss, leading to widespread adoption. Early plugs, such as Harvey Hubbell's separable attachment plug patented in 1913, allowed detachable connections to existing light sockets, marking a key step toward portable appliance use. By 1928, the addition of a grounding prong by inventor Philip F. Labre enhanced safety by providing a path for fault currents, forming the foundation for three-prong grounded outlets still common today. Global standardization of AC power plugs and sockets is overseen by bodies like the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC), which defines types through specifications such as IEC 60884-1 for household plugs and sockets rated above 50 V AC. In North America, the National Electrical Manufacturers Association (NEMA) establishes dimensional and performance standards for plugs, receptacles, and related components used in residential, commercial, and industrial settings, covering configurations from 15 A at 125 V to higher ratings. Approximately 15 primary plug types (A through O) exist worldwide, differentiated by pin count, shape, and spacingâsuch as Type A (two flat parallel blades) in the United States or Type F (two round pins with side grounding clips) in much of Europe. These variations stem from historical national preferences, resulting in no single universal design and necessitating adapters for cross-border compatibility. Voltages for AC systems typically range from 100 V to 240 V, with 120 V at 60 Hz standard in North America and 230 V at 50 Hz prevalent in Europe, Asia, and Africa, reflecting early 20th-century decisions by utilities and governments. Safety features are integral to modern standards, including earthing (grounding) contacts to divert stray currents, polarized designs to prevent reverse polarity, and innovations like ground fault circuit interrupters (GFCIs) that detect imbalances as small as a few milliamperes and cut power to avert shocks in wet environments. For industrial applications, standards like IEC 60309 specify robust, color-coded plugs and sockets rated up to 800 A and 1,000 V, often with interlocking mechanisms to prevent disconnection under load.
